title: When a City Stream Comes Back
subject: rla
passage:
For decades, a narrow city stream had been treated almost like a drainage ditch. Concrete walls kept the channel straight, and several small barriers interrupted the flow. After heavy rain, water moved through the channel quickly. During dry weeks, some sections became shallow and warm, and few plants grew along the banks.

A restoration project began with work that was easy for visitors to miss. Utility lines near the stream had to be relocated before excavation could begin. Crews then widened two sections of the channel and added gentle bends. The goal was to slow the water in some places and create a wider range of depths. Native plants were added along the banks after the new channel shape was complete. Months later, workers removed two low barriers that had prevented fish from moving between sections of the stream.

The first year produced encouraging but uneven results. During several moderate storms, water spread into the widened sections instead of rising as sharply inside the old narrow channel. However, the largest storm of the year still flooded a nearby path. Biologists also recorded more insects and small fish in restored areas. They described the ecological results as promising rather than final because that year had unusually mild summer temperatures, which may also have helped aquatic life.

The project created a different problem once a walking path beside the stream became popular. People stepped off the path to reach the water, damaging some of the newly planted banks. Rather than close the path, the city installed short fencing near the most fragile areas and added signs directing visitors to two durable access points. Plant damage decreased during the following months while path use remained high.

The city also installed simple water-level markers near the path so staff could compare photographs after storms. Those observations are not treated as substitutes for sensor data, but they help the team notice where debris collects and where visitors are most likely to encounter high water. The information is added to the same annual review as the biological and engineering measurements.

The restoration team plans to monitor the stream for at least four more years. Engineers will compare how the channel responds to storms of different sizes. Biologists will track fish, insects, water temperature, and plant survival. The team says the project should be judged as a system rather than by one result. A wider channel may reduce some flood pressure without preventing every flood, and more fish in one mild year do not prove that every ecological change came from restoration. The design will continue to be adjusted as new evidence appears.

questions.prompt: Which event had to occur before crews could begin reshaping the channel?
questions.explanation: The passage says utility lines had to be relocated before excavation could begin.
questions.rule: Look for a required earlier condition, not just any earlier event.

options.text: Utility lines were relocated
Native plants were added
options.whyWrong: “Native plants were added” is placed at the wrong point in the sequence. Check what happens immediately before and after the target event.

options.text: Fish barriers were removed
options.whyWrong: “Fish barriers were removed” is placed at the wrong point in the sequence. Check what happens immediately before and after the target event.

options.text: The walking path became popular
options.whyWrong: “The walking path became popular” is placed at the wrong point in the sequence. Check what happens immediately before and after the target event.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Utility lines near the stream had to be relocated before excavation could begin. Crews then widened two sections... Native plants were added ... Months later, workers removed two low barriers.

questions.prompt: How did the restored channel perform differently during moderate storms and the largest storm?
questions.explanation: The moderate storms showed reduced pressure, while the largest storm still produced flooding.
questions.rule: Compare the same outcome - storm response - across both conditions.

options.text: It prevented all flooding during both kinds of storms
options.whyWrong: “It prevented all flooding during both kinds of storms” treats the subjects as similar in a way the text does not support.

options.text: It reduced sharp water rise during moderate storms, but the largest storm still flooded a nearby path
It flooded the path during moderate storms but not during the largest storm
options.whyWrong: “It flooded the path during moderate storms but not during the largest…” assigns the two subjects’ features to the wrong sides of the comparison.

options.text: The stream became completely dry during both kinds of storms
options.whyWrong: “The stream became completely dry during both kinds of storms” treats the subjects as similar in a way the text does not support.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: During several moderate storms, water spread into the widened sections ... However, the largest storm ... still flooded a nearby path.

questions.prompt: Why do the biologists describe the ecological results as promising rather than final?
questions.explanation: The unusually mild summer is another factor that could affect aquatic life, so the restoration cannot yet be credited for every change.
questions.rule: Notice alternative causes before making a strong causal claim.

options.text: Mild summer temperatures could also have contributed to the observed changes
They counted no fish at all
options.whyWrong: “They counted no fish at all” treats one coincidence as a meaningful pattern without enough supporting evidence.

options.text: The project had already ended
options.whyWrong: “The project had already ended” assigns a motive that the text never gives. Use only motives supported by actions or wording.

options.text: Native plants were never installed
options.whyWrong: “Native plants were never installed” reverses cause and effect. The passage presents the relationship in the opposite direction.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: They described the ecological results as promising rather than final because that year had unusually mild summer temperatures, which may also have helped aquatic life.

questions.prompt: What can the reader infer about the restoration team's approach to evidence?
questions.explanation: The team monitors multiple outcomes over years, uses cautious language, and says the design will be adjusted as new evidence appears.
questions.rule: Combine clues across the passage and choose the smallest supported inference.

options.text: The team prefers to make permanent conclusions from one observation
options.whyWrong: “The team prefers to make permanent conclusions from one observation” could be possible, but the passage does not provide enough evidence to support that conclusion.

options.text: The team treats unexpected problems as proof that restoration should stop
options.whyWrong: “The team treats unexpected problems as proof that restoration should…” could be possible, but the passage does not provide enough evidence to support that conclusion.

options.text: The team expects to revise its interpretation and design as more evidence is collected
The team measures only how the stream looks to visitors
options.whyWrong: “The team measures only how the stream looks to visitors” conflicts with a specific detail in the passage.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: The team says the project should be judged as a system rather than by one result.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage as a whole?
questions.explanation: The passage presents benefits, limits, confounding factors, visitor impacts, and a plan for continued monitoring.
questions.rule: A conclusion should fit the whole pattern, including qualifications.

options.text: Stream restoration succeeds only when walking paths are closed
options.whyWrong: “Stream restoration succeeds only when walking paths are closed” goes beyond the scope of the text. The evidence supports a narrower claim.

options.text: The project has solved every flooding and ecological problem
options.whyWrong: “The project has solved every flooding and ecological problem” predicts an outcome the passage does not establish.

options.text: The mild summer proves the restoration had no ecological effect
options.whyWrong: “The mild summer proves the restoration had no ecological effect” relies too heavily on one detail instead of combining the relevant clues.

options.text: The restoration shows several benefits, but its effects vary by condition and require continued monitoring and adjustment

questions.evidenceExcerpt: The team says the project should be judged as a system rather than by one result.

questions.prompt: How does increased public use of the walking path affect the restoration project?
questions.explanation: Visitor behavior creates a new problem and prompts a management response designed to protect plants while preserving access.
questions.rule: Use a relationship verb: public use creates a problem that changes management.

options.text: It causes the city to remove all native plants
options.whyWrong: “It causes the city to remove all native plants” reverses how the two ideas or events are connected in the passage.

options.text: It causes plant damage that leads the city to add fencing and designated access points
It has no effect on management decisions
options.whyWrong: “It has no effect on management decisions” connects details that the passage does not present as meaningfully related.

options.text: It directly causes moderate storms
options.whyWrong: “It directly causes moderate storms” connects details that the passage does not present as meaningfully related.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: People stepped off the path ... damaging ... banks. Rather than close the path, the city installed short fencing ... Plant damage decreased ... while path use remained high.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses an idea developed throughout the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage follows a staged project, several kinds of evidence, new problems, and future monitoring.
questions.rule: A central idea should account for the entire passage, not one result.

options.text: The best stream projects focus only on fish counts
options.whyWrong: “The best stream projects focus only on fish counts” focuses on one detail rather than the broader conclusion supported by the text.

options.text: Concrete channels should always be removed from every city
options.whyWrong: “Concrete channels should always be removed from every city” generalizes beyond the examples or conditions described in the text.

options.text: Restoring an urban stream requires staged changes, multiple measures of success, and continued adjustment as new results appear
Walking paths are the main cause of urban flooding
options.whyWrong: “Walking paths are the main cause of urban flooding” is reasonable but incomplete; it leaves out another important part of the passage.
